{"id": "cc28daab-0515-47f6-9280-b3ec913a5ded", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "A tcpdump taken on my EC2 instance shows 20,000-byte TCP segments even though the instance MTU is 9001. Is the MTU misconfigured?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "e29789b5-2def-4a72-b39d-593925cceb3e", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_rOy0CMfB7yusorCuM82UDT", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Nitro system considerations for performance tuning\",\"context\":\"#### Application design considerations\\n\\nThere are aspects of application design and configuration that can affect your\\nprocessing efficiency. The following list includes some important\\nconsiderations.\\n\\n**Packet size**\\n: Larger packet sizes can increase throughput for the data that an\\n instance can send and receive on the network. Amazon EC2 supports jumbo\\n frames of 9001 bytes, however other services may enforce different\\n limits. Smaller packet sizes can increase the packet process rate,\\n but this can reduce the maximum achieved bandwidth when the number\\n of packets exceed PPS allowances.\\n\\n If the size of a packet exceeds the Maximum Transmission Unit\\n (MTU) of a network hop, a router along the path might fragment it.\\n The resulting packet fragments are considered exceptions, and are\\n normally processed at the standard rate (not accelerated). This can\\n cause variations in your performance. However, you can override the\\n standard behavior for outbound fragmented packets with the fragment\\n proxy mode setting. For more information, see Maximize network performance on your Nitro system. We recommended that\\n you evaluate your topology when you configure MTU.\\n\\n**Protocol trade-offs**\\n: Reliable protocols like TCP have more overhead than unreliable\\n protocols like UDP. The lower overhead and simplified network\\n processing for the UDP transport protocol can result in a higher PPS\\n rate, but at the expense of reliable packet delivery. If reliable\\n packet delivery isn\u2019t critical for your application, UDP might be a\\n good option.\\n\\n**Micro-bursting**\\n: Micro-bursting occurs when traffic exceeds allowances during brief\\n periods of time rather than being evenly distributed. This typically\\n happens on a microsecond scale.\\n\\n For example, say that you have an instance that can send up to 10\\n Gbps, and your application sends the full 10 Gb in half a second.\\n This micro-burst exceeds the allowance during the first half second\\n and leaves nothing for the remainder of the second. Even though you\\n sent 10Gb in the 1 second timeframe, allowances in the first half\\n second can result in packets being queued or dropped.\\n\\n You can use a network scheduler such as Linux Traffic Control to\\n help pace your throughput and avoid causing queued or dropped\\n packets as a result of micro-bursting.\\n\\n**Number of flows**\\n: A single flow is limited to 5\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ena-nitro-perf.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot packet loss on my VPN connection?\",\"context\":\"### Identify issues with the network or application\\n\\nGet simultaneous packet captures on both the EC2 instance and the on-premises host when the issue occurs. Use the packet capture to identify issues with the network or application.\\n\\nTo get a packet capture for Linux instances, use **tcpdump**.\\n\\nTo install **tcpdump** on Amazon Linux, run the following command:\\n\\n```plaintext\\nsudo yum install tcpdump\\n```\\n\\nTo install **tcpdump** on Ubuntu, run the following command:\\n\\n```plaintext\\nsudo apt-get install tcpdump\\n```\\n\\nFor Windows, instead of **tcpdump**, use Wireshark. To download the tool, see [Download Wireshark](https://www.wireshark.org/download.html) on the Wireshark website.\\n\\nThe packet capture looks similar to the following example:\\n\\n```plaintext\\ntcpdump -i any -nnvv port 500 and port 4500\\ntcpdump: listening on any, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), capture size 65535 bytes\\n18:12:54.944933 IP (tos 0x0, ttl 63, id 43082, offset 0, flags [DF], proto UDP (17), length 212)\\n10.20.20.80.500 > 23.20.145.20.500: [udp sum ok] isakmp 1.0 msgid 00000000 cookie 19e7adeabfefca84\u21920000000000000000: phase 1 I ident:\\n(sa: doi=ipsec situation=identity\\n(p: #1 protoid=isakmp transform=1\\n(t: #1 id=ike (type=lifetype value=sec)(type=lifeduration value=7080)(type=enc value=aes)(type=keylen value=0080)(type=auth value=preshared)(type=hash value=sha1)(type=group desc value=modp1024))))\\n(vid: len=16)\\n(vid: len=16)\\n(vid: len=16)\\n(vid: len=16)\\n(vid: len=16) out slot1/tmm0 lis=$_ike_1061b_out_23.20.145.20 port=1.0 trunk=\\n18:12:54.946069 IP (tos 0x0, ttl 253, id 56278, offset 0, flags [none],\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/troubleshoot-vpn-packet-loss\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Troubleshoot the Elastic Network Adapter Windows driver\",\"context\":\"##### Considerations for using jumbo ethernet frames\\n\\nJumbo frames allow more than 1500 bytes of data by increasing the payload size per packet,\\nwhich increases the percentage of the packet that is not packet overhead. Fewer packets are\\nneeded to send the same amount of usable data. However, traffic is limited to a maximum MTU\\nof 1500 in the following cases:\\n\\n* Traffic outside of a given AWS Region for EC2 Classic.\\n* Traffic outside of a single VPC.\\n* Traffic over an inter-Region VPC peering connection.\\n* Traffic over VPN connections.\\n* Traffic over an internet gateway.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nPackets over 1500 bytes are fragmented. If you have the `Don't Fragment`\\nflag set in the IP header, these packets are dropped.\\n\\nJumbo frames should be used with caution for internet-bound traffic, or any traffic\\nthat leaves a VPC. Packets are fragmented by intermediate systems, which slows down\\nthis traffic. To use jumbo frames inside of a VPC without impacting outbound traffic\\nthat's leaving the VPC, try one of the following options:\\n\\n* Configure the MTU size by route.\\n* Use multiple network interfaces with different MTU sizes and different routes.\\n\\n###### Recommended use cases for jumbo frames\\n\\nJumbo frames can be useful for traffic inside of and between VPCs. We recommend\\nusing jumbo frames for the following use cases:\\n\\n* For instances that are collocated inside of a cluster placement group, jumbo\\n frames help to achieve the maximum network throughput possible. For more\\n information, see Placement groups for your Amazon EC2 instances.\\n* You can use jumbo frames for traffic between your VPCs and your on-premises\\n networks over Direct Connect. For more information about using Direct Connect, and verifying\\n jumbo frame capability, see MTU for private virtual interfaces or transit virtual interfaces in\\n the *Direct Connect User Guide*.\\n* For more information about supported MTU sizes for transit gateways, see\\n Quotas for your\\n transit gateways in the *Amazon VPC Transit Gateways*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/troubleshoot-ena-driver.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify AWS EC2 tcpdump behavior showing TCP segments larger than interface MTU"}

{"id": "2c15f7c6-0db5-4fb2-995f-939734a86b04", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No, that's almost certainly not a misconfiguration — it's an artifact of how tcpdump captures traffic relative to NIC offloading.

**What's happening:**

- With TCP Segmentation Offload (TSO) / Generalized Segmentation Offload (GSO), the kernel hands the NIC driver one large buffer (which can be tens of KB) instead of pre-splitting it into MTU-sized frames. The actual segmentation into MTU-sized frames happens in the ENA driver/hardware right before the data hits the wire.
- tcpdump typically captures at a point in the stack *before* that final segmentation occurs (it attaches above the driver), so it logs the large, pre-segmented buffer as if it were a single "packet" — even though what actually goes out on the wire is split into 9001-byte (or smaller) frames matching your MTU.
- This is standard, expected Nitro/ENA driver behavior, not a sign that oversized packets are hitting the network.

**How to confirm:**
- Capture with `-s 0` and check: does the capture show the TCP `DF` (Don't Fragment) flag along with a length well above the MTU, but no fragmentation errors or retransmits? That's consistent with offload, not a real MTU problem.
- Capture on the actual wire/peer side (e.g., at the destination instance, or on a VPC Traffic Mirroring / packet capture that sits downstream of segmentation) — you should see properly MTU-sized frames there.
- You can also temporarily disable TSO/GSO (`ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off`) and re-run tcpdump; the 20,000-byte "segments" should disappear and you'll see normal 9001-byte-or-smaller frames, confirming it was an offload artifact.

So unless you're also seeing actual connectivity issues, retransmits, or black-holed traffic, I wouldn't treat this as an MTU misconfiguration — it's just where in the stack the capture is happening. If you are seeing real packet loss or fragmentation errors alongside this, that'd be worth digging into separately.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
